title: Status Epilepticus: The Neurological & Neuro-Ophthalmic Emergency
summary: Status Epilepticus (SE) is a critical medical emergency defined by prolonged seizure activity or recurrent seizures without return to baseline. This infographic outlines the rapid-fire management protocols, neuro-ophthalmic manifestations, and evidence-based pharmacotherapy required for resident and fellow mastery.

data.title: Status Epilepticus: The Neurological & Neuro-Ophthalmic Emergency
data.summary: Status Epilepticus (SE) is a critical medical emergency defined by prolonged seizure activity or recurrent seizures without return to baseline. This infographic outlines the rapid-fire management protocols, neuro-ophthalmic manifestations, and evidence-based pharmacotherapy required for resident and fellow mastery.

rows: Continuous activity >5 min or ≥2 seizures without recovery. t2 marks risk of long-term damage.
Focal awareness or impaired awareness seizures without recovery.
Prolonged altered consciousness with generalized spike-wave on EEG.
Rhythmic motor activity, tonic-clonic movements, impaired consciousness.
Altered mental status, 'Twilight state', mild eyelid myoclonus.
Automatisations, staring, focal EEG changes, aphasia.
Failure of 1st and 2nd line drugs; SE continuing >24 hrs despite anesthetics.

sections.title: Neuro-Ophthalmic Examination Findings
content: Ictal Eye Deviation: Eyes usually deviate AWAY from the focus in destructive lesions, but TOWARDS the focus during ictus.
Nystagmus-like movements: Rapid eye jerking (Epileptic nystagmus) can occur in focal SE.
Pupillary Changes: Mydriasis or sluggish reactivity is common during the ictal phase.
Post-ictal Findings: Transient Horner's Syndrome or gaze palsy (Todd's paralysis of eye movements).
Fundus: Look for papilledema (suggests raised ICP as etiology) or chorioretinal scars (suggests TORCH infections).

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Molecular Failure
content: 1. Failure of GABA-ergic Inhibition: GABA-A receptors are internalized (trafficked out of the synapse).
2. Over-activation of Glutamate: NMDA and AMPA receptors are mobilized to the synapse, increasing excitation.
3. Depletion of Neuropeptides: Depletion of inhibitory peptides like Substance P.
4. Neuronal Damage: Excessive Calcium influx leads to excitotoxicity and mitochondrial failure within 30-60 mins.

rows: Asynchronous movements, eye closure (forceful), side-to-side head shaking, no post-ictal period.
Prodromal 'dimming' of vision, brief duration, immediate recovery of consciousness.
Extensor response due to brainstem herniation, fixed/blown pupils (unlike most SE).
Visual 'scintillating scotomas' (positive symptoms), slow progression (minutes, not seconds).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: Step 1: Point-of-Care Glucose (Rule out Hypoglycemia immediately).
Step 2: Stat Labs (CBC, BMP, LFTs, Calcium, Magnesium, Tox Screen).
Step 3: Emergent Neuroimaging (Non-contrast Head CT to rule out ICH/Mass).
Step 4: Continuous EEG (Essential for diagnosing Non-Convulsive SE).
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture (If febrile or immunosuppressed, after checking for mass effect).

content.explanation: Lorazepam (Ativan) 4mg IV (repeated once) is the drug of choice. If no IV access: Midazolam 10mg IM (RAMPART Trial).

rows: Excellent safety profile, few drug interactions.
Avoid in pregnancy or liver failure.

sections.title: Phase 3: Refractory SE (Anesthetic Phase)
content: Midazolam (Dormicum): Bolus 0.2mg/kg followed by infusion (0.05-2mg/kg/hr).
Propofol (Diprivan): Bolus 1-2mg/kg followed by infusion (2-10mg/kg/hr). Beware Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS).
Ketamine: NMDA antagonist (Bolus 1-2mg/kg). Useful as receptor profile changes in late SE.
Phenobarbital: Bolus 15-20mg/kg. Strong sedation, risk of respiratory depression.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Threats
content: Airway Obstruction / Hypoxia: Intubate early if Benzodiazepines cause respiratory drive failure.
Hyperthermia: Sustained SE can cause rhabdomyolysis and core temps >40°C.
Herniation Signs: Fixed dilated pupil or Cushing's Triad (Bradycardia, Hypertension, Irregular Breathing).
Propofol Infusion Syndrome: Metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac failure.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Evidence Base
sections.content: The ESETT Trial (2019) demonstrated that Levetiracetam, Fosphenytoin, and Valproate are equally effective for benzodiazepine-refractory SE (approx. 50% success). The RAMPART Study (2012) proved that IM Midazolam is superior to IV Lorazepam in the pre-hospital setting due to faster administration times.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Don't wait for EEG to start treatment if clinical suspicion is high.
Pseudo-Status: If the patient is 'resistant' to eye opening, consider PNES.
Aggressive treatment is key: Every minute of seizure increases the risk of pharmacoresistance.
In patients with known epilepsy, the most common trigger is low AED levels/non-compliance.

sections.title: Long-Term Prognosis & Complications
content: Permanent Cognitive Deficits: Memory impairment (hippocampal sclerosis).
Systemic: Pulmonary edema, cardiac arrhythmias, and acute kidney injury (from rhabdo).
Mortality: Highest in the elderly and those with stroke or hypoxia as the etiology.
Recurrence: Approx. 15-20% chance of another SE episode.
